identity.title: A is for Absorption: Studying Feature Splitting and Absorption in Sparse Autoencoders

problem.claim: The paper studies whether SAEs robustly decompose LLM activations into interpretable hierarchical features as SAE feature count increases.

gap.claim: The abstract identifies a lack of robustness in sparse decomposition and feature splitting, including monosemantic features failing to fire where expected.

contributions.claim: Defines feature absorption: parent-like features are absorbed into their hierarchical child features under sparse decomposition.
Introduces a metric for detecting feature absorption in SAEs.
Reports that changing SAE size or sparsity is insufficient to resolve absorption, and discusses potential approaches to its theoretical issues.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors state that they coin the term feature absorption for this phenomenon and introduce a detection metric.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that seemingly monosemantic features sometimes fail to activate where expected and instead become absorbed into child features.
The authors report empirical validation of their findings on hundreds of LLM SAEs.
The authors report that varying SAE sizes or sparsity does not solve the issue.

narrative_sequence.summary: SAEs are framed as tools for decomposing LLM activation spaces into interpretable features.
Increasing SAE feature count is associated with hierarchical features splitting into finer-grained features.
The paper reports that splitting is not robust and characterizes parent-feature failure as absorption into child features, linked to sparsity optimization.
It introduces an absorption metric, reports validation across hundreds of SAEs, and argues that size or sparsity variation is insufficient.
The paper discusses implications and possible routes toward addressing the underlying theoretical issues.

source_observation.claim: The abstract names a specific failure mode, identifies a proposed cause, and pairs it with a metric and empirical validation.

lessons.interpretation: A precise failure-mode–cause–measurement chain can make an interpretability claim more diagnostically useful than reporting aggregate decomposition quality alone.
lessons.application: For a new representation-learning study, define a concrete failure mode, hypothesize its mechanism, and introduce a targeted diagnostic before presenting broad evaluation.
lessons.exception: This framing is less suitable when the task has no identifiable failure mode or when mechanism claims cannot be separated from descriptive measurement.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the absorption metric, its threshold or validation procedure.
The number, model diversity, and evaluation conditions of the hundreds of LLM SAEs are unspecified.
The proposed approaches for resolving the theoretical issues are not described in detail.
